kurals.tamil:
அழிவதூஉம் ஆவதூஉம் ஆகி வழிபயக்கும்
ஊதியமும் சூழ்ந்து செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhivadhooum aavadhooum aaki vazhipayakkum,
Oodhiyamum soozhndhu seyal.
kurals.meaning: Before you act, weigh what will be lost, what will be gained, and the net benefit that will follow afterwards; only then undertake the action.
kurals.elementary: Before you start something, ask three questions: What might I lose? What will I get? And after everything is added up, will it really be worth it? Only when you have thought about all three should you begin.
kurals.university: The opening couplet sets out a three-part calculus that governs the whole chapter: அழிவது (what is spent or destroyed at the outset — the cost), ஆவது (what comes into being — the gain), and வழிபயக்கும் ஊதியம் (the profit that results in due course — the net yield after costs are subtracted). The verb சூழ் (to deliberate, to survey all round) is the chapter’s keyword. Parimelazhagar reads the triad as capital outlay, return, and eventual surplus, which makes this one of the earliest cost-benefit formulations in world ethical literature. Placed in the Porul (polity) section, the kural is addressed first to rulers, but it is phrased generally enough to apply to any undertaking. The point is not to avoid risk but to see the whole ledger before committing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhagavad Gita 18.25 describes “tamasic” action as action begun out of delusion, without regard to its consequences, the loss it will cause, the injury to others, and one’s own capacity.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna ranks actions by the quality of mind behind them. The lowest kind is the one started blindly, without counting cost, consequence, harm, or whether you are even able to do it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita lists the very factors the Kural tells us to weigh (loss, outcome, capacity) and condemns action that ignores them.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual match: 18.25 names anubandha (consequence), kshaya (loss), himsa (injury) and paurusha (capacity). Paraphrased; translation wording not web-verified this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses an everyday picture: no sensible builder starts a tower without first sitting down and working out whether he can afford to finish it.
christianity.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s instruction to reckon cost against outcome before starting.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match. Standard KJV wording reproduced from the received text; could not be re-verified against a web copy this session (search budget exhausted), so flagged is_quote false pending check.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught his companions the istikhara prayer for every matter of consequence: before deciding, one asks God for the better course, naming whether the matter is good or bad “for my religion, my livelihood and the outcome of my affairs.”
islam.explanation: Muslims are taught to pause before important decisions and ask God to guide them toward what is good in its consequences and away from what is harmful.
islam.tie_back: Istikhara builds a deliberate pause and a weighing of outcomes into the start of any undertaking, as the Kural requires.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘pause and weigh outcomes before acting’ structure, but istikhara is a prayer for divine guidance rather than a human cost-benefit calculation. Paraphrase.

judaism.quote_or_event: Alexander the Great asked the Elders of the South who deserves to be called wise. They answered: the one who sees what will result (ha-ro’eh et ha-nolad) — who anticipates the consequences of his conduct.
judaism.explanation: For the rabbis, wisdom isn’t just knowing a lot; it’s seeing ahead to what your actions will produce.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘வழிபயக்கும் ஊதியம்’ — what an action yields down the road — is exactly what the rabbis’ wise man foresees.
judaism._accuracy_note: Passage located on Sefaria via search; wording given as a paraphrase of the Sefaria/Steinsaltz translation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells his son Rahula to reflect before any bodily, verbal or mental act: would this lead to my own affliction, to the affliction of others, or both? If so, it is unskillful and should not be done; if not, it may be done.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches a child to use his actions like a mirror — look at them before, during and after, and check whether they will cause harm.
buddhism.tie_back: A formal ‘check before you act’ procedure, weighing results before committing, like the Kural.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close structural match; the Buddhist test weighs moral harm rather than material gain and loss. Paraphrase.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus (‘Forethought’) warned his brother Epimetheus (‘Afterthought’) never to accept a gift from Zeus; Epimetheus accepted Pandora anyway and only understood the harm once it had come.
greek_mythology.explanation: The two brothers’ names say it all: one thinks before, the other thinks after. The one who thinks after lets disaster into the world.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural asks us to be Prometheus — to calculate outcomes before acting, not after.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good thematic contrast of forethought versus afterthought; the myth is about heeding a warning rather than an explicit cost-benefit weighing. Paraphrase.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Benjamin Franklin’s “moral or prudential algebra”: divide a sheet into Pro and Con columns, list the reasons on each side over several days, strike out items of equal weight against each other, and see where the balance lies before deciding.
philosophy.explanation: Franklin gave a friend a practical method for hard decisions: write down everything for and against, cancel out equal items, and see what remains.
philosophy.tie_back: A literal written version of the Kural’s ledger of loss, gain, and resulting profit.
philosophy.source: Benjamin Franklin, letter to Joseph Priestley, 19 September 1772
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close method match; Franklin weighs reasons rather than strictly material costs. Paraphrase.

kurals.tamil:
தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணிச் செய்வார்க்கு
அரும்பொருள் யாதொன்றும் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Therindha inaththotu therndhennich cheyvaarkku,
Arumporul yaadhondrum il.
kurals.meaning: For those who act after deliberating carefully with well-chosen counsellors, and after examining the matter themselves, nothing is too difficult to achieve.
kurals.elementary: If you pick good, trustworthy friends, talk your plan over with them, and think it through yourself too, there is almost nothing you cannot get done.
kurals.university: The couplet joins two acts of discernment: தெரிந்த இனம் (a circle that has itself been tested and chosen — echoing the preceding chapters on seeking the help of the great and avoiding mean company, 44–46) and தேர்ந்து எண்ணி (having examined and reasoned). Counsel is only as good as the counsellors, so selection comes before consultation. The strong universal claim (‘no object is hard to attain’) is typical of Valluvar’s rhetoric, which states the ideal case to motivate the practice. The idea of the ruler’s council (mantra) was a central institution of classical Indian statecraft, and the Kural places it at the heart of deliberate action.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya opens his chapter on counsel by teaching that all undertakings of state should be preceded by deliberation in a properly constituted council, and that counsel should be kept secret and taken with tested ministers.
hinduism.explanation: India’s classic manual of government says a king should never act on big matters alone: he should first talk them through with carefully chosen, trustworthy advisers.
hinduism.tie_back: Same pairing as the Kural: chosen counsellors plus deliberation before action.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match in subject and setting (statecraft). Paraphrase of the Shamasastry translation; not web-verified this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.”
christianity.explanation: Plans fail when people make them alone; they succeed when many wise advisers help shape them.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s promise that consultation makes goals achievable.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match; Proverbs stresses number of counsellors where the Kural stresses their quality. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an describes the believers as those “whose affair is [determined by] consultation among themselves” (shura).
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises communities that decide their shared matters by talking them over together rather than by one person’s whim.
islam.tie_back: Shura is the Islamic institution of deliberating with others before acting.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on consultation; the Qur’an does not add the Kural’s claim that nothing is then impossible. Wording from Sahih International as remembered; not re-verified online this session.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.”
judaism.explanation: A nation without good advice collapses; with many wise advisers it stays safe.
judaism.tie_back: Same principle as the Kural, applied to national affairs.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match; shares Hebrew Bible source with the Christian entry. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When King Ajatasattu plans to attack the Vajjians, the Buddha says they will prosper and not decline so long as they meet together often, meet in harmony, and conduct their business in harmony.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a people who regularly gather and decide things together, in agreement, will be very hard to defeat.
buddhism.tie_back: Collective, well-ordered deliberation makes a group strong, as in the Kural.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Communal assembly rather than a leader consulting chosen advisers; partial match. Paraphrase.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Volunteering for the night raid on the Trojan camp, Diomedes asks for a companion, saying that when two go together one sees the advantage before the other, while a man alone has thinner wit; he picks Odysseus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Diomedes chooses the cleverest partner he can find, because two minds notice what one would miss.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Choosing the right companion to think with before a risky action is the Kural’s point.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match: both selection of a counsellor and joint deliberation. Paraphrase.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “We deliberate not about ends but about means.” Aristotle adds that on important questions we call in others to help us deliberate, distrusting our own ability to decide alone.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says real deliberation is working out how to reach a goal, and for big decisions sensible people ask others for help.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s deliberation with others mirrors the Kural’s deliberation with a chosen circle.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.3 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: The quoted sentence was confirmed in the Ross translation via search; the follow-on point about calling in others is paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
ஆக்கம் கருதி முதலிழக்கும் செய்வினை
ஊக்கார் அறிவுடை யார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aakkam karudhi mudhalizhakkum seyvinai,
Ookkaar arivutai yaar.
kurals.meaning: The wise will not attempt an undertaking that, in the hope of future profit, risks losing the capital they already have.
kurals.elementary: Smart people don’t risk everything they already have just because they hope to win something bigger. They protect what they have first.
kurals.university: The pairing ஆக்கம் (gain, increase) and முதல் (principal, capital) is commercial vocabulary and continues the ledger of 461. The verb ஊக்கார் (‘they will not be eager to / will not set about’) matters: Valluvar does not ban all risk, but says the wise will not be enthusiastic for ventures where the principal itself is at stake. This is a rule of prudence rather than timidity. It tells a ruler not to gamble the treasury or the kingdom’s security on speculative expansion. Later chapters praise energy and persistence (ஊக்கம், chapter 60), so the teaching is best read as ‘secure the base before seeking growth’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A saying attributed to Chanakya warns that whoever abandons what is certain in pursuit of what is uncertain loses the certain, and the uncertain is lost as well.
hinduism.explanation: If you drop what you surely have to chase something you only might get, you can end up with nothing.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s warning against losing capital while chasing gain.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close match. Paraphrased; translations vary and the verse number differs across editions. Attribution to the historical Kautilya is traditional, not certain.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want.”
christianity.explanation: Careful planners end up with plenty, but people who rush after quick gain end up poor.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it contrasts steady, careful increase with hasty ventures that lead to loss.
christianity._accuracy_note: Related but more general: about haste versus diligence, not specifically about risking principal. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

islam.quote_or_event: On wine and gambling (maysir) the Qur’an says there is great sin in them and some benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.
islam.explanation: The Qur’an admits gambling can bring some gain, but says the harm is bigger, so it should be given up.
islam.tie_back: Gambling is the clearest case of risking what one has for hoped-for profit, which the Kural tells the wise to avoid.
islam._accuracy_note: The Qur’an’s reasoning is moral and religious, not purely prudential; the connection runs through the gamble-for-gain example. Paraphrase.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Isaac taught that a person should always divide his money into three parts: a third in land, a third in merchandise, and a third kept at hand.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud advises spreading your wealth so no single venture can wipe you out.
judaism.tie_back: Protecting the principal while still seeking gain is the practical heart of the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Practical match (risk management); the Talmud prescribes diversification rather than refusal of risky ventures. Paraphrase.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha advises the householder Sigala to divide his wealth into four parts: one to enjoy, two to invest in his work, and the fourth to keep in reserve against misfortune.
buddhism.explanation: Even the Buddha told lay people to save part of their money for hard times instead of putting it all at risk.
buddhism.tie_back: Keeping a reserve so that the principal survives is the Kural’s concern.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Prudent household economics; related, not identical. Paraphrase.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable, a dog carrying a piece of meat across a stream sees its reflection, snaps at the ‘bigger’ piece in the water, and drops the real one.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greedy dog lost the meat it had by grabbing for a bigger piece that wasn’t real.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A vivid picture of losing capital while reaching for imagined gain.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Dog and Its Reflection’ (Perry 133)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match, but Aesop is Greek fable literature rather than mythology proper; used as the closest Greek narrative parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is, therefore, only a madman who, in a calm, would pray for a storm; a wise man's way is, when the storm does come, to withstand it with all the means at his command, and especially, when the advantages to be expected in case of a successful issue are greater than the hazards of the struggle.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero warns against exposing oneself to danger needlessly and says a risk is worth running only when the gain to be expected from success outweighs what is hazarded.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the Kural's rule that the wise weigh what may be lost against what may be gained, and do not court ruin for the sake of a hoped-for profit.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book I, §83 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Miller, Loeb 1913, De Officiis I.61-91). Partial match: Cicero speaks of danger in war and public affairs, not of risking one's capital in business, but the principle of weighing hazard against expected advantage is the same.

kurals.tamil:
தெளிவி லதனைத் தொடங்கார் இளிவென்னும்
ஏதப்பாடு அஞ்சு பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thelivi ladhanaith thotangaar ilivennum,
Edhappaatu anju bavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who fear the disgrace of failure will not begin any undertaking whose outcome and means are not clear to them.
kurals.elementary: People who care about their good name don’t start things they don’t fully understand, because failing halfway would make them look foolish.
kurals.university: தெளிவு (clarity, certainty) is the key concept: an undertaking is ‘தெளிவு இலது’ when its means, outcome, or one’s own ability to finish it are uncertain. The motive for restraint is இளிவு (humiliation, contempt), described as an ஏதப்பாடு (a harm or calamity). Valluvar treats reputation as a real asset of the ruler, and public failure as damage to it, not just wounded pride. Commentators differ slightly. Parimelazhagar stresses that the doubtful venture ends in ridicule, while modern commentators such as Kalaignar read it more broadly as avoiding dishonourable acts. Both readings rest on the same logic: foreseeable shame is itself a cost to include in deliberation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna warns Arjuna that people will speak of his dishonour forever, and that for one who has been honoured, dishonour is worse than death.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reminds Arjuna that a respected person has a reputation to protect, and losing it is a terrible thing.
hinduism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s view of disgrace as a grave harm that must shape one’s choices.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Weak match: Krishna uses fear of disgrace to push Arjuna into acting, whereas the Kural uses it as a reason not to begin unclear ventures. Best available Hindu parallel on disgrace as a practical cost. Paraphrase.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says the builder who starts without checking his resources will be laughed at when the half-built tower stands unfinished.
christianity.tie_back: The very same motive the Kural gives: fear of public ridicule for an unfinished undertaking.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an commands: do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge; hearing, sight and heart will all be questioned.
islam.explanation: Don’t go after something you don’t really understand, because you will be held responsible for how you used your senses and mind.
islam.tie_back: Forbids acting without clear knowledge, as the Kural does, though the motive is accountability to God rather than fear of shame.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the ‘no clarity, no action’ half; the motive differs. Paraphrase.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Go not forth hastily to strive, lest thou know not what to do in the end thereof, when thy neighbour hath put thee to shame.”
judaism.explanation: Don’t rush into a dispute you aren’t sure how to finish, or you’ll end up embarrassed in front of others.
judaism.tie_back: Same logic as the Kural: an unclear beginning leads to shame at the end.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on both uncertainty and shame. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says a deed is not well done if one regrets it afterwards and reaps its fruit weeping; it is well done if one does not regret it and reaps its fruit with joy.
buddhism.explanation: A good action is one you won’t be sorry for later.
buddhism.tie_back: Thinking ahead to avoid later regret and grief is close to the Kural’s concern with avoiding later disgrace.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Focuses on inner remorse rather than public disgrace; partial match. Paraphrase.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Bellerophon, after his triumphs, tried to ride Pegasus up to Olympus; Pegasus threw him, and he ended his life wandering alone and scorned.
greek_mythology.explanation: A hero tried something far beyond his reach and ended up disgraced and alone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An undertaking begun without regard to its real prospects ends in humiliation, as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The myth is mainly about hubris toward the gods; the link to deliberation and disgrace is indirect. Paraphrase.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises: in every affair consider what comes before and what follows, then undertake it; otherwise you will begin eagerly, and when difficulties appear you will give up shamefully.
philosophy.explanation: Think a project through first, or you’ll start with excitement and quit in embarrassment.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s link between lack of clarity at the start and disgrace at the end.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match. Paraphrase; Enchiridion numbering follows the standard edition.

kurals.tamil:
வகையறச் சூழா தெழுதல் பகைவரைப்
பாத்திப் படுப்பதோ ராறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Vakaiyarach choozhaa thezhudhal pakaivaraip,
Paaththip patuppadho raaru.
kurals.meaning: To rise against enemies without thoroughly planning every aspect of the campaign is a way of planting them in a prepared bed where they will grow strong.
kurals.elementary: If you rush to fight someone without planning properly, you actually help them — like planting a seed in good soil and watering it so it grows bigger.
kurals.university: The metaphor is agricultural. பாத்தி is a prepared garden bed, and பாத்திப் படுத்தல் means settling a plant in such a bed so it takes root. A poorly planned attack does not just fail. It strengthens the enemy, who gains confidence, allies, and legitimacy from beating back a rash assault. வகையற (exhaustively, covering every category) points to the sixfold considerations of statecraft (strength, place, time, means, allies, and so on) that commentators read into the phrase. Pope renders it: ‘With plans not well matured to rise against your foe, / Is way to plant him out where he is sure to grow!’ It is the chapter’s one explicitly military couplet.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya teaches that before marching, the conqueror must assess his own and the enemy’s relative strength, the suitability of place and time, the season for campaigning, and possible revolts and losses.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra says a king should work out many factors before going to war, not just whether he is angry or brave.
hinduism.tie_back: An itemised version of the Kural’s ‘வகையற’ — deliberating every category before rising against a foe.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match in subject and genre. Paraphrase; not web-verified this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: A wise king works out whether his army can win before he marches. If it can’t, he seeks peace instead.
christianity.tie_back: Same scenario as the Kural: deliberate fully before rising against an enemy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an instructs the believers to prepare against their enemies whatever strength they can, including steeds of war, so as to deter them.
islam.explanation: Muslims are told to get properly ready before facing an enemy, not to rush in unprepared.
islam.tie_back: Preparation before confrontation is the Kural’s point, though the Qur’an stresses deterrence.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the preparation theme; lacks the Kural’s image of the rash attack strengthening the enemy. Paraphrase.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Every purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war.” And: “For by wise counsel thou shalt make thy war.”
judaism.explanation: The Bible says plans hold up when made with advice, and that war especially should be waged only with good counsel.
judaism.tie_back: Directly applies deliberation before action to going to war.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Before attacking the Vajjians, King Ajatasattu sends his minister Vassakara to ask the Buddha. After hearing the seven conditions that keep the Vajjians strong, the minister concludes they cannot be defeated by force alone.
buddhism.explanation: Even an ambitious king checked first whether his attack could work, and the answer showed him it couldn’t.
buddhism.tie_back: A narrative case of assessing an enemy’s strength before rising against it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: The sutta’s purpose is teaching communal virtue, not military planning; the deliberation-before-war framing is incidental. Paraphrase.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Adrastus led the Seven against Thebes although the seer Amphiaraus foresaw that the expedition would fail. Six of the seven champions died, and Thebes held.
greek_mythology.explanation: An army marched against a city despite warnings that the plan was doomed, and it was destroyed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A rash, ill-considered attack that failed and left the enemy secure, as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology.source: Apollodorus, Library 3.6; Aeschylus, Seven Against Thebes
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on a rash campaign ending in disaster; the ‘planting the enemy’ image is not present. Paraphrase.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu observes that the general who wins makes many calculations in his temple before the battle is fought, while the general who loses makes but few calculations beforehand.
philosophy.explanation: Battles are mostly won or lost in the planning, before any fighting starts.
philosophy.tie_back: Near-identical doctrine: exhaustive calculation before engaging the enemy.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, ch. 1 (tr. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close match. Classical Chinese military philosophy used as the philosophical parallel. Paraphrase of Giles; not web-verified this session.

kurals.tamil:
செய்தக்க அல்ல செயக்கெடும் செய்தக்க
செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seydhakka alla seyak ketum seydhakka,
Seyyaamai yaanung ketum.
kurals.meaning: One is ruined by doing what ought not to be done, and one is equally ruined by failing to do what ought to be done.
kurals.elementary: You can get into trouble in two ways: by doing something you shouldn’t, and by not doing something you should. Both can hurt you just as much.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a chiastic repetition of செய்தக்க (‘what is fit to be done’). It balances sins of commission against sins of omission and treats both as equally ruinous (கெடும் … கெடும்). This keeps the chapter from turning into a counsel of timidity: deliberation is meant to discern the right action, and paralysis is as fatal as rashness. In a political reading, a ruler who neglects necessary measures (defence, justice, relief) falls as surely as one who pursues reckless ones. The same double structure is familiar from moral and legal traditions that separate positive duties from prohibitions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Laws of Manu state that a man who omits a prescribed act, or performs a blameworthy act, or clings to sensual objects, must perform a penance.
hinduism.explanation: In the Hindu law books you can go wrong both by skipping your duties and by doing forbidden things, and both need to be put right.
hinduism.tie_back: Same two-sided account of wrongdoing as the Kural.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match; Manu speaks of ritual and moral penance, the Kural of worldly ruin. Paraphrase.

christianity.quote_or_event: The General Confession: “We have left undone those things which we ought to have done; And we have done those things which we ought not to have done.”
christianity.explanation: Anglican worshippers confess both kinds of failure: what they neglected and what they wrongly did.
christianity.tie_back: An almost word-for-word counterpart to the Kural’s two clauses.
christianity.source: Book of Common Prayer (1662), Morning Prayer, General Confession
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match (the Confession is about sin, the Kural about ruin). Well-known liturgical wording; not re-verified online this session.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an calls for a community “inviting to [all that is] good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong,” and says those are the successful.
islam.explanation: Muslims are asked both to promote what is good and to stop what is wrong. Doing only one isn’t enough.
islam.tie_back: The paired duties of doing right and avoiding wrong echo the Kural’s two-sided rule.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel two-sided structure, but addressed to the community’s duty toward others rather than the individual’s own acts and omissions. Wording from memory; not re-verified online this session.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Simlai taught that 613 commandments were given to Moses: 365 prohibitions, matching the days of the year, and 248 positive commands, matching the limbs of the body.
judaism.explanation: Jewish law is built from both ‘do this’ and ‘don’t do that’ commandments, and a person can fail by breaking either kind.
judaism.tie_back: The positive/negative split mirrors the Kural’s ‘what should be done’ and ‘what should not be done’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the double structure but is a legal classification rather than a warning about ruin. Paraphrase.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To avoid all evil, to cultivate good, and to cleanse one’s mind — this is the teaching of the Buddhas.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha’s teaching in one line: stop doing bad things and start doing good things, and keep your mind pure.
buddhism.tie_back: Avoiding the wrong and doing the right, the Kural’s two clauses in the same order.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match. Buddharakkhita wording given from memory; not re-verified online this session.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles withdraws from the fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon and refuses to return even when the Greeks are being routed. His inaction leads to the death of Patroclus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles’ refusal to act when he was needed brought disaster on his own side and on his best friend.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the second half of the Kural: ruin from failing to do what ought to be done.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates only the omission half of the couplet; best available mythic narrative. Paraphrase.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Mill writes that a person may cause evil to others not only by his actions but by his inaction, and in either case is justly accountable to them for the injury.
philosophy.explanation: Mill says you can harm people by what you fail to do as well as by what you do, and you are responsible either way.
philosophy.tie_back: A modern philosophical statement of the Kural’s parity between commission and omission.
philosophy.source: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859), ch. 1
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match. Mill speaks of harm to others, the Kural of self-ruin. Paraphrase; not web-verified this session.

kurals.tamil:
எண்ணித் துணிக கருமம் துணிந்தபின்
எண்ணுவம் என்பது இழுக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ennith thunika karumam thunindhapin,
Ennuvam enbadhu izhukku.
kurals.meaning: Think carefully, then resolve upon a course of action; to say ‘we will think about it after we have begun’ is a disgrace.
kurals.elementary: Do your thinking first, then make up your mind and go. Starting first and figuring it out later is a big mistake.
kurals.university: Probably the most-quoted couplet of the chapter. Its force comes from the sequence எண்ணி → துணிக (reflect → resolve) and the rejection of the reversed order துணிந்தபின் எண்ணுவம் (‘having resolved, we shall reflect’). Two faults are excluded at once. One is beginning without deliberation. The other, implied, is wavering and reopening the question after committing, which dissipates resolve. துணிவு means both decision and courage, so the couplet unites prudence and boldness: deliberation belongs before action, and firmness belongs after decision. இழுக்கு (a slip, a blemish) casts the failure as a lapse of character, not merely of technique.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After eighteen chapters of dialogue, Arjuna tells Krishna that his delusion is destroyed, his doubts are gone, and he stands firm, ready to act on Krishna’s word.
hinduism.explanation: The whole Gita is one long pause to think before battle. Only when Arjuna’s doubts are cleared does he commit to action.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s structure (deliberation first, then firm resolve) is the Kural’s sequence.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good structural match; the Gita’s deliberation is spiritual instruction rather than practical planning. Paraphrase.

christianity.quote_or_event: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”
christianity.explanation: Once you’ve committed to something important, you mustn’t keep looking back and second-guessing.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s condemnation of reconsidering after resolving.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the second half (no wavering after commitment); Luke 14:28 elsewhere covers the first half. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

islam.quote_or_event: “…and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah.”
islam.explanation: God tells the Prophet: talk things over with your people first, but once you’ve decided, act with trust and don’t hesitate.
islam.tie_back: An exact counterpart: consult and deliberate, then resolve and proceed firmly.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one sequence match. Sahih International wording from memory; not re-verified online this session.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee. Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established.”
judaism.explanation: Think carefully about where you are going, then walk steadily ahead without turning aside.
judaism.tie_back: Pondering first and then holding firmly to the path is the Kural’s order.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha describes the resolve of a disciple who has set out on the path: willingly let only skin, sinews and bones remain, let flesh and blood dry up; energy will not be relaxed until the goal is attained.
buddhism.explanation: Once a Buddhist practitioner decides to seek awakening, they commit completely and don’t turn back.
buddhism.tie_back: Illustrates the unwavering resolve that should follow deliberation.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Captures only the firm-resolve half; the deliberation half is not explicit. Best available Buddhist parallel. Paraphrase.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the Cyclops’s cave, Odysseus first thinks of stabbing Polyphemus as he sleeps, but a second thought stops him: no one could move the boulder from the door. He devises the stake-and-ram plan and carries it out without hesitation.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus thinks through his options before he acts, then sticks to the plan he chooses.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus’s metis is the Kural’s ‘think, then resolve’ in action.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Descartes’s second maxim: be as firm and resolute in action as possible once a course is chosen, like travellers lost in a forest who should walk straight in one direction rather than wander in circles.
philosophy.explanation: Descartes says that once you’ve picked a direction, keep going; changing your mind every few steps gets you nowhere.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s rule against reopening deliberation after resolving.
philosophy.source: René Descartes, Discourse on Method (1637), Part 3
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match on post-decision firmness. Paraphrase.

kurals.tamil:
ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம் பலர்நின்று
போற்றினும் பொத்துப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aatrin varundhaa varuththam palarnindru,
Potrinum poththup patum.
kurals.meaning: Effort not spent in the proper way will fail, even if many people stand by to support and protect the work.
kurals.elementary: If you work hard but in the wrong way, the project will fall apart — even if lots of people are trying to help hold it together.
kurals.university: ஆறு here means ‘way, proper method’. வருந்தா வருத்தம் (‘toil not toiled [in the right way]’) is effort poured out without a method. The verb போற்று (to guard, cherish, maintain) and பலர்நின்று (many standing together) anticipate the objection that sheer numbers or goodwill can make up for bad method. Valluvar denies it. பொத்துப் படும் means ‘it will spring a leak / be breached’, an image of a vessel or dam giving way. The couplet adds to the chapter’s argument: deliberation must choose not only whether to act but how, and a wrong method cannot be rescued by resources applied afterwards.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna says that one who discards the injunctions of scripture and acts on the impulse of desire attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.
hinduism.explanation: If you ignore the proper way and just do what you feel like, your effort won’t bring success.
hinduism.tie_back: Effort outside the proper method (ஆறு) is fruitless, as the Kural says.
hinduism._accuracy_note: The Gita’s ‘proper way’ is scriptural ordinance, the Kural’s is practical method; partial match. Paraphrase.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus compares the one who hears his words and does not do them to a foolish man who built his house on sand: the rain fell, the floods came, the winds beat on it, and it fell, and great was its fall.
christianity.explanation: However much work goes into a house, it collapses if it isn’t built the right way on a solid foundation.
christianity.tie_back: Labour without the right method ends in collapse, the Kural’s ‘breach’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good image of method-failure, though Jesus’ point is about obeying his teaching. Paraphrase.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an speaks of the greatest losers in their deeds: those whose effort is lost in worldly life while they think they are doing well in their work.
islam.explanation: Some people work very hard and even think they’re doing great, but their effort is wasted because it isn’t on the right path.
islam.tie_back: Effort outside the right way is lost, however sincere, as the Kural says.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on ‘misdirected effort comes to nothing’; the Qur’anic context is religious rather than practical. Paraphrase.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct.”
judaism.explanation: Chopping wood with a dull axe takes much more effort; a little wisdom about the right method saves a lot of wasted strength.
judaism.tie_back: Wrong method multiplies toil; right method (wisdom) makes it succeed, as the Kural says.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on method versus brute effort. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Bhumija that one who seeks oil by pressing sand will get none, whether he has hopes or not, because that is not the way to get oil; one who presses sesame seeds will get it.
buddhism.explanation: No matter how hard or hopefully you squeeze sand, you won’t get oil. You need the right method.
buddhism.tie_back: An exact parallel: the outcome depends on the method, not on effort or wishes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match (the sutta applies it to spiritual practice). Paraphrase.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld the Danaids are condemned to carry water forever in leaking vessels, so the jar they labour to fill never fills.
greek_mythology.explanation: They work without end, but because their jars have holes, all their effort is wasted.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Endless labour through a ‘breached’ vessel echoes the Kural’s பொத்துப் படும் (springs a leak).
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Mainly an image of futile labour as punishment, not of wrong method; kept for the leak image. Weak match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Francis Bacon observes that a lame man who keeps to the right road outstrips a runner who takes the wrong one.
philosophy.explanation: Going the right way matters more than how fast or strong you are.
philosophy.tie_back: Method beats force, the Kural’s core claim.
philosophy.source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum (1620), Book I, Aphorism 61
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match. Paraphrase; not web-verified this session.

kurals.tamil:
நன்றாற்ற லுள்ளுந் தவறுண்டு அவரவர்
பண்பறிந் தாற்றாக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Nandraatra lullun thavaruntu avaravar,
Panbarin dhaatraak katai.
kurals.meaning: Even in doing good there can be failure, if one acts without understanding the particular nature of each person concerned.
kurals.elementary: Even being kind can go wrong if you don’t understand the person you’re helping. What helps one person might upset another.
kurals.university: The couplet carries deliberation into benevolence itself. நன்று ஆற்றல் (doing good, conferring benefits) is normally praised without qualification, but Valluvar notes a தவறு (error, failure) that arises when one does not know அவரவர் பண்பு (the respective natures of each person). Parimelazhagar explains that benefits given to those whose nature does not suit them may be misused or may turn them hostile. For a ruler, rewards and favours are tools of policy and must fit their recipients. The reduplicated அவரவர் (‘each respectively’) insists on individual discernment rather than uniform treatment. Some editions spell the verb தவுறுண்டு; the standard reading is தவறுண்டு.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra, a bird in her snug nest advises shivering monkeys in the rain to build shelters for themselves; the offended monkeys tear her nest apart.
hinduism.explanation: The bird meant well, but she gave advice to creatures who couldn’t take it, and she lost her home.
hinduism.tie_back: Doing good without knowing the recipient’s nature backfires, exactly as the Kural warns.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book 1 (‘The Monkeys and the Bird’)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match. Story title and placement vary by recension. Paraphrase.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.”
christianity.explanation: Don’t offer something precious to those who can’t value it, or they may trample it and turn on you.
christianity.tie_back: Good things given without regard to the recipient’s nature can do harm, as the Kural says.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

islam.quote_or_event: Ali ibn Abi Talib said: speak to people according to what they can understand; do you want Allah and His Messenger to be denied?
islam.explanation: Even true teaching can backfire if it doesn’t fit what the listener can grasp.
islam.tie_back: Doing good (teaching truth) must fit each person’s capacity, as the Kural teaches.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match, limited to teaching. A statement of Ali recorded by al-Bukhari rather than a Prophetic hadith. Paraphrase.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.”
judaism.explanation: The same correction that a wise person welcomes will make a scornful person hate you.
judaism.tie_back: Whether a well-meant act helps or harms depends on the recipient’s character.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha explains to Prince Abhaya that he speaks only what is true and beneficial, and even then he knows the proper time for saying it, taking account of the listener.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha didn’t just say true, helpful things. He chose when and how to say them depending on who was listening.
buddhism.tie_back: Good speech must be adapted to the person and occasion, as the Kural requires of good deeds.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on discernment in doing good; limited to speech. Paraphrase.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Helios, wishing to prove his love, swears to grant his son Phaethon any gift; Phaethon asks to drive the sun chariot, cannot control the horses, scorches the earth, and is struck down by Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: A father’s generous gift, given without thinking about whether his son could handle it, led to disaster.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A kindness given without regard to the recipient’s nature and capacity brings ruin, the Kural’s warning.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that giving or spending money is easy and anyone can do it, but doing it to the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive and in the right way is neither easy nor for everyone.
philosophy.explanation: Being generous is easy; being generous well — to the right person in the right way — takes wisdom.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s point that good deeds need discernment about the person.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.9 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match. Paraphrase of Ross; not web-verified this session.

kurals.tamil:
எள்ளாத எண்ணிச் செயல்வேண்டும் தம்மொடு
கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ellaadha ennich cheyalventum thammotu,
Kollaadha kollaadhu ulagu.
kurals.meaning: One should think carefully and do only what will not bring the world’s scorn; for the world will not approve of what does not befit one’s own position and character.
kurals.elementary: Before you act, ask: will good people respect this, and does it fit who I am? People won’t accept actions that don’t suit the person doing them.
kurals.university: The closing couplet adds a social test to the practical tests of the preceding kurals. எள்ளாத (‘what is not despised’) introduces public judgement, and the wordplay கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது (‘the world will not accept what is not accepted with oneself’) sets the criterion of fit. An action must suit the agent’s station, capacity and character (தம்மொடு). Parimelazhagar takes it that the world will not approve deeds out of keeping with one’s status, even when the deeds themselves are not bad. For a ruler, legitimacy depends on acting in ways subjects and peers can recognise as fitting. The chapter thus ends by setting individual calculation inside a community of judgement.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna teaches that it is better to perform one’s own duty (svadharma), even imperfectly, than another’s duty well; and that whatever a great person does, others follow as their standard.
hinduism.explanation: Do what fits your own role and nature, and remember that people watch and copy those in high positions.
hinduism.tie_back: Action fitting one’s own station, judged by the watching world, echoes தம்மொடு கொள்ளாத.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good match on ‘befitting oneself’; the public-scorn element is only implicit. Paraphrase.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul speaks of “providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says it isn’t enough to be right before God; your conduct should also look honourable to other people.
christianity.tie_back: Acting in ways the world will not scorn is the Kural’s standard too.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on public reputation; lacks the ‘befitting one’s station’ element. Standard KJV wording, not re-verified online this session.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said: righteousness is good character, and sin is what wavers in your soul and you would dislike people to find out about.
islam.explanation: One test of wrongdoing is whether you’d be embarrassed for others to learn of it.
islam.tie_back: Uses the imagined judgement of others as a check on action, like the Kural’s ‘what the world will not scorn’.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on the public-judgement test; the hadith is about sin, not suitability to station. Paraphrase.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi said: which is the right path a person should choose? Whatever is an honour to the one who does it and brings him honour from others.
judaism.explanation: Pick the way of acting that you can respect in yourself and that other people will respect too.
judaism.tie_back: The same two tests as the Kural: fitting to oneself, and approved by the world.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match. Paraphrase of the Sefaria translation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kalama Sutta the Buddha tells the Kalamas that when they know for themselves that certain things are unskillful, blameworthy and criticised by the wise, and lead to harm, they should abandon them.
buddhism.explanation: One way to check an action is to ask whether wise people would criticise it.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Criticised by the wise’ is the Buddhist form of the Kural’s ‘what the worthy would not scorn’.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on the social test; the sutta pairs it with personal verification. Paraphrase.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Arachne, a mortal weaver, challenges the goddess Athena and weaves the gods’ misdeeds; her presumption is punished and she is turned into a spider.
greek_mythology.explanation: Arachne did something that didn’t fit her place in the world, and she was punished for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates action out of keeping with one’s station meeting rejection, the Kural’s கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak match: the myth concerns hubris toward the gods, not public disapproval of unbecoming conduct. Best available Greek parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Adam Smith argues that we judge our own conduct by imagining how an impartial spectator would view it, and that we naturally desire not only to be praised but to be praiseworthy.
philosophy.explanation: Smith says a good check on our actions is to picture how a fair-minded observer would see them.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘act so that the world will not scorn’ is a version of Smith’s impartial-spectator test.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), Part III
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good match on public judgement as a guide; Smith internalises the spectator, whereas the Kural points to actual social reception. Paraphrase.
